courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: You flip a fair coin twice. Let A = "first flip is heads" and B = "the two flips match". Are A and B independent?
options: No, because B depends on the first flip
Yes: P(A and B) = 1/4 = P(A) P(B)
No, because A and B can both happen
It cannot be determined without more data
explain: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HH or TT), and P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B). Even though B is defined using the first flip, it is independent of A. Independence is checked with numbers, not by whether one event is mentioned in the other's definition.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
question: Batch size 64 gives a gradient-estimate standard deviation of s (per coordinate, i.i.d. examples). Approximately what does batch size 256 give?
options: s, since batch size does not affect noise
explain: The mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so its standard deviation scales as 1/sqrt(batch). Four times the batch gives sqrt(4) = 2 times less noise, so s/2. The variance falls by 4.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
question: Prior Beta(3, 3). You observe 2 heads and 6 tails. What are the posterior and its MAP estimate?
options: Beta(5, 9), MAP 1/3
Beta(2, 6), MAP 0.25
Beta(5, 9), MAP 0.25, the same as the MLE
Beta(3, 3), since one small sample does not change the prior
explain: Add heads to a and tails to b: Beta(3 + 2, 3 + 6) = Beta(5, 9). MAP = (5 - 1) / (5 + 9 - 2) = 4/12 = 1/3, pulled from the MLE of 0.25 toward the prior's 0.5.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
question: Your budget is fixed. You decide to make the model 3 times larger than planned. What must happen to the number of training tokens?
options: It stays the same, compute depends only on N
It must triple
It must drop to one third
It must drop to one ninth
explain: With $C \approx 6ND$ fixed, $D = C/(6N)$, so tripling N cuts D to one third. Compute depends on both knobs; nothing about the product is squared.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
question: Which is the best summary of the Kaplan vs Chinchilla disagreement?
options: Chinchilla showed loss does not follow power laws
They agree that loss is a power law, but differ on how to split compute; replications trace Kaplan's split to experimental setup
Kaplan used more compute so its result is more reliable
The difference is only because they used different tokenizers
explain: Both papers find smooth power-law trends. The disagreement is the compute-optimal exponent (0.73 vs about 0.5), and later work explains it by schedule, parameter counting, small scale and optimizer details. Kaplan actually used smaller models than Chinchilla.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
question: A service builds each prompt as system_text + user_text and encodes it with `enc.encode(prompt, allowed_special="all")`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; allowed_special only changes how decoding works
It is slower, but the ids are identical either way
It raises ValueError on every prompt
A user who types a special string such as <|endoftext|> gets the real control token, so their text can end the document or fake structure the model trusts
explain: allowed_special="all" turns every special string in the text into its control id, including strings typed by users. Allow special tokens only in text you wrote, and encode user text with the defaults (which raise) or with disallowed_special=() so it stays plain text.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: Why does He initialization use 2 / fan-in rather than Xavier's 1 / fan-in (equal fans) for ReLU layers?
options: ReLU doubles the gradient on the positive side
The factor 2 accounts for the bias term
ReLU zeroes about half of a symmetric pre-activation, halving the mean square, and the factor 2 cancels that
Larger weights train faster, so 2 is a safe speed-up
explain: With zero-mean symmetric pre-activations, ReLU keeps only the positive half, so the average of $\mathrm{relu}(z)^2$ is $\mathrm{Var}(z)/2$. Multiplying Var(w) by 2 restores a per-layer factor of exactly 1.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Mixed precision: fp16, bf16 and loss scaling
question: Your gradients include many values around 1e-9 and you want to avoid a loss scaler. Which format works, and what does it give up?
options: fp16, because subnormals reach down past 1e-9
bf16: fp32's exponent range keeps 1e-9 representable, at the cost of only 7 mantissa bits (spacing 0.0078 near 1)
fp16, because it has more mantissa bits than bf16
Either one: both have 8 exponent bits
explain: fp16's smallest positive number is 2^-24, about 6e-8, so 1e-9 rounds to 0 unless the loss is scaled. bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits, so range is not the problem; precision is, which is why the weights stay in fp32.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: A run's loss sits at 2.30 (10 classes) for 300 steps. Every layer's update-to-weight ratio is about 1e-8, and the activation std drops about 8x per layer. Most likely cause?
options: Weights initialized far too small, so the signal and gradients vanish
A learning rate 30x too high
model.eval() was never called
Dropout is too strong
explain: A constant ln 10 loss means the network predicts uniformly. The per-layer scale collapse matches lesson 1's analysis of a too-small init, and ratios of 1e-8 mean the weights are effectively frozen. A too-high rate gives large ratios and climbing gradient norms instead.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
question: Which of these runs a third-party package's own code on your machine before your application ever imports it?
options: Installing an npm package that has a postinstall script, with scripts enabled
Reading the package's README on the registry website
Running npm ls
Installing a pure-Python wheel with pip
explain: Lifecycle scripts run during install. A wheel is unpacked without running package code (though a .pth file it installs runs at the next Python start).

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Build system compromise: SolarWinds, CCleaner and 3CX
question: SUNSPOT replaced a source file only while MsBuild was running and restored it afterwards. Which check would most likely have exposed it?
options: Verifying the code-signing signature on the shipped DLL (dynamic-link library, a Windows code file)
Code review of the git repository
Running unit tests
Rebuilding the same commit on an independent builder and comparing hashes
explain: The repository was clean and the signature was genuine. Only something that compares the build output against an independent build of the same source sees the difference.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
question: Why does keyless signing reduce the damage of a CI compromise compared with a GPG key stored as a CI secret?
options: Fulcio scans artifacts for malware before signing
There is no long-lived private key to steal; each key lives for one signature, and every signing event is publicly logged
Keyless signatures do not need verification
Sigstore signatures cannot be forged even by the signer
explain: An attacker inside the job could still sign during that run, but they cannot walk away with a key that works for months, and their signing is visible in Rekor. Compare HashiCorp's forced key rotation after Codecov.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
question: Which control would most directly have stopped Jia Tan from shipping 5.6.0 alone?
options: Running unit tests in CI
Signing release tarballs
Requiring a second maintainer to review and approve every release and the release archive contents
Using SHA-256 instead of CRC in xz
explain: The releases were signed and tests passed. A second, independent person checking that the release archive matched the reviewed git tree is the control aimed at a single trusted insider, which SLSA's Source track formalises as required review.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls
question: You generate 10x more synthetic training text from the same teacher with top-p 0.9. Under the tail-cutting model, when does this stop improving the student?
options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: A lab wants its 2027 pretraining mix to stay anchored to human text. Which plan does this lesson support best?
options: Keep pre-LLM snapshots and other known-human sources permanently in the mix, and treat classifier or watermark filtering of new crawls as an extra layer
Rely on an AI-text classifier to remove all model-written pages from new crawls, then drop the old snapshots to save space
Rely on watermarks, since every model that writes web text embeds one
Ignore provenance, since accumulating any data at all prevents every form of collapse
explain: Detectors can be evaded by paraphrasing and are bounded by how close AI text is to human text, and watermarks cover only cooperating generators. Known-human data kept permanently is the anchor that does not depend on detection. Accumulation bounds error but does not by itself protect the tails.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
question: strace -c on a busy program shows 2 million read calls taking 4 s of system time. Without strace, the program's total run time is 1.5 s. What is the best reading?
options: The program spends 4 s in read; strace measures it exactly
strace double-counts calls made by threads
read must be served by the vDSO in the untraced run
The call count is trustworthy, but strace's own overhead inflates the times, so measure time without it
explain: Tracing stops the program around every call, so times under strace are inflated; strace(1) warns that a traced process runs more slowly. The count of 2 million is what the program really does, and it suggests a bigger buffer. read has no vDSO version.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: Your team wants a fleet-wide p99 dashboard. Each of 40 hosts exports its own p99 every minute. What should you do?
options: Average the 40 p99 values, weighting by request count
Take the maximum of the 40 p99 values, which is exactly the fleet p99
Export histogram bucket counts from each host, sum them, and compute p99 from the merged histogram
Take the median of the 40 p99 values to ignore outlier hosts
explain: Percentiles are not additive; neither the weighted mean nor the max of per-host p99s equals the fleet p99 in general. Summed histogram counts describe the combined distribution, so the percentile computed from them is right up to bucket resolution.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: At month granularity with half-open intervals, role X is Jan 2020 to Jun 2020 and role Y is Jul 2020 to Dec 2020 (both as written, inclusive). Which Allen relation holds for X relative to Y?
options: before, because June is before July
overlaps, because they share the month boundary
during
meets
explain: As half-open intervals X is [2020-01, 2020-07) and Y is [2020-07, 2021-01). X's exclusive end equals Y's start, which is the definition of meets: back-to-back, no gap and no overlap.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
question: Your majority-vote accuracy on a math benchmark stops improving between N = 64 and N = 512, but pass@512 (checked against the answer key) keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?
options: Samples become correlated at large N
On the unsolved problems the correct answer is a minority answer, so adding votes reinforces the wrong mode
The model runs out of context window
pass@k is computed incorrectly at large N
explain: Majority vote converges to the mode of the answer distribution. For problems where a wrong answer is the mode, more samples raise coverage but not voting accuracy. That is the plateau Brown et al. report.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: Which of these changes the trained weights of a network itself at inference, instead of a per-sequence state that starts fresh for every input?
options: A TTT-Linear layer reading a 10,000-token prompt
Linear attention accumulating v k-transpose over a document
LaCT updating its SwiGLU fast weights once per 2048-token chunk
Sun et al. (2019): one rotation-prediction gradient step on each test image before classifying it
explain: Sun et al. update the classifier's own shared parameters with a self-supervised loss on the test image. The other three are fast weights: a TTT layer's W, linear attention's state and LaCT's fast weights all start from a learned or zero initial value for each sequence and are thrown away afterwards, while the network's ordinary weights stay frozen.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In MAC, why does segment 3's attention not see the memory update made from segment 3's own tokens?
options: Because the memory is read before the segment is written: h comes from M_2, and the write that adds segment 3 happens after attention
Because MAC never writes segment tokens into the memory
Because persistent tokens block the memory during segment 3
Because the memory is only updated at the end of the sequence
explain: MAC's order is retrieve, attend, write, gate. Retrieval reads M_(t-1), from before the segment, so attention combines the compressed past with the exact current segment. Only the final gate reads the freshly written M_t.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: A service spends 50 ns per malloc inside a global allocator lock. Ignoring everything else, what is the most mallocs per second the whole machine can do through that lock?
options: 20 million per second, regardless of core count
20 million per second per core
It depends only on how fast each core runs application code
Unlimited, since a mutex costs nothing when uncontended
explain: One holder at a time, 50 ns each: $1/(50 \text{ ns}) = 2 \times 10^7$ per second for the whole machine. More cores add waiters, not throughput.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: An application runs 4,000 threads on a 32-CPU machine, most of them blocked most of the time. Which allocator front-end is the better fit for memory footprint, and why?
options: Per-thread caches, because blocked threads release their caches automatically
Per-CPU caches, because the number of caches is bounded by the 32 CPUs rather than the 4,000 threads
Neither: a global lock is best when threads are mostly blocked
Per-thread caches, because rseq does not work with more threads than CPUs
explain: Per-thread caches keep idle objects in every thread's cache, including the thousands of sleeping ones, or must shrink each cache until it is useless. Per-CPU caches exist only per logical CPU, so at most 32 hold memory, and the running threads share them.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
question: You stack 'process opened a handle to LSASS' across 3,000 machines. One backup agent made 50,000 such events, all on a single server, so sorted by count() it looks like the most common program. Which aggregation shows it is present on only one machine?
options: Sorting by time instead of by count
dcount(DeviceId) per process, the number of distinct devices
count() of events per process
sum of event sizes per process
explain: Counting distinct devices measures prevalence: a value seen on one device stays at 1 however many events that device produces, so the backup agent rises into the rare list next to the other one-machine programs, where a person can confirm it is the expected server. Counting raw events lets any chatty process look 'common' and sink out of a least-frequent list.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
question: A Volt Typhoon-style actor copied ntds.dit with ntdsutil and then deleted the copy. Which evidence from the hunt plan most likely still records where the copy was written?
options: Event 1102
ESENT events 216, 325, 326 and 327 in the Application log
The PortProxy registry key
The firewall log
explain: AA23-144A notes that the ESENT events' details should contain the file path where the copies were created, and that this 'can greatly aid in a hunt operation' because the files themselves can be deleted. Event 1102 would only show that a log was cleared, and the port proxy and firewall evidence concern a different behaviour.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: A hunt team spends a month hunting for encoded PowerShell, which already has a tested production rule that fires reliably. What does TaHiTI suggest they should have done first?
options: Checked the state of existing detections to avoid hunting for activity that traditional detection already covers
Hunted only for file hashes
Nothing; repeating hunts is always good
Bought a new EDR
explain: TaHiTI says continuous insight into the state of detection mechanisms is required 'to avoid hunting for malicious activity that is already covered'. Hunting time is scarce; spend it where the coverage map is empty or untested.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth
question: Your SOC confirmed 40 malicious domains last quarter. A paid feed of 2 million domains contained 12 of them, all also present in your free ISAC feed. What does this measurement show?
options: The paid feed is the most valuable because it is the largest
The paid feed added no unique detections against what you saw last quarter; check whether it serves another requirement before renewing
The ISAC feed must be wrong because it is smaller
Both feeds should be dropped because neither had all 40
explain: Unique contribution was zero against confirmed activity, so the feed's value, if any, lies elsewhere (another PIR, earlier delivery, or threats you have not yet seen). Size says nothing about relevance, and no feed will contain everything, so missing some confirmed domains is expected.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
question: A 2024 advisory tags log clearing as T1070.001. Your 2026 detection list (ATT&CK v20) has a rule tagged T1685.005. What is the right conclusion?
options: They are unrelated techniques
They describe the same behaviour under different ATT&CK versions; translate the ID before measuring coverage
The advisory is wrong
T1685.005 must be deprecated
explain: In ATT&CK v20, T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs redirects to T1685.005 under Disable or Modify Tools. Mappings are version-specific, so compare like with like.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
question: In April 2021 the US named the SVR; in April 2022 Mandiant merged UNC2452 into APT29. Why might a vendor take a year longer than a government?
options: Vendors are not allowed to attribute
The vendor only reached the conclusion once its own firsthand evidence supported it, while the government could draw on intelligence sources a company does not have
The government statement was wrong
APT29 did not exist before 2022
explain: Mandiant said its merge was 'based on firsthand data gathered by Mandiant'. Governments can use signals and human intelligence that are not public, which supports the sponsor rung earlier but cannot be checked by outsiders.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
question: Your adversary list contains only 'anonymous internet attacker'. What does the model most likely miss?
options: Denial-of-service attacks
Attacks on the encryption of web traffic
Phishing emails
Misuse by people who already have legitimate access
explain: Insiders start inside the trust boundary with real credentials. Anonymous internet attackers can attempt denial of service, phishing and network attacks, so those are not the gap.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
question: You can spend money on one defence. Which helps the root of an attack tree most?
options: Raising the cost of the branch that is currently cheapest
Raising the cost of the most expensive branch
Adding a new leaf to every branch
Whichever defence is cheapest to buy
explain: The root of an OR tree equals its cheapest branch. Raising any other branch leaves the root unchanged. Price matters, but only after you know which branch it changes.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
question: FireEye raised alerts on 30 November and 2 December, yet data kept leaving until mid-December. What does this teach about defence in depth?
options: A detection layer only counts if someone acts on it: detection without response is not a working layer
FireEye was the wrong product
Detection is useless against skilled attackers
Alerts should be turned off to reduce noise
explain: The signal was there. The response process failed. The next lesson shows why layers that share a failure, such as one ignored alert queue, add less protection than they appear to.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: A CXL device is onlined through the dax kmem driver, but firmware provides no HMAT or CDAT performance data. Which tier does its node join?
options: memory_tier4, the same tier as DRAM, so it is never a demotion target
memory_tier22, from the kmem default adistance of 5 x 576 = 2880
The slowest possible tier, because it has no CPUs
None: the kernel refuses to online memory without performance data
explain: drivers/dax/kmem.c starts from MEMTIER_DEFAULT_DAX_ADISTANCE (5 x 576 = 2880) and only overrides it if a performance-based algorithm can compute one. 2880 / 128 = 22.5, so tier 22. Memory onlined as ordinary system RAM instead defaults to 576 and would share tier 4 with DRAM.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
question: On the test year, seasonal naive has MAE 24.25 and naive has MAE 37.92. What would most directly remove seasonal naive's remaining error on this series?
options: Use a smaller alpha
Switch from MAE to RMSE
Use only the last 12 months of training data
Add a trend term, since all its errors are positive by roughly one year of growth
explain: Every seasonal naive error is positive, between 19 and 30, close to 12 months x 2 per month = 24. That is a systematic bias from ignoring the trend. A method with both trend and season terms (Holt-Winters, next lesson) addresses it. Changing the metric changes the score, not the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
question: Which handshake messages in TLS 1.3 can a passive observer read in plaintext?
options: ClientHello, ServerHello and Certificate
Only ClientHello and ServerHello
None; everything is encrypted from the first byte
All of them; only application data is encrypted
explain: RFC 9846 encrypts every handshake message after ServerHello. The two Hello messages must be in clear because the keys do not exist until both key shares have been exchanged.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
question: A server supports TLS 1.2 and SSL 3.0 and implements TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV. Interference on the path causes a browser to fall back and retry with SSL 3.0. What happens?
options: The server accepts SSL 3.0, because the client asked for it
The browser detects the attacker's TCP reset and alerts the user
The server silently upgrades the connection to TLS 1.2
The server sees the SCSV, knows it supports a higher version than offered, and aborts with inappropriate_fallback
explain: The SCSV tells the server "this is a fallback retry". If the server could have done better, a fallback means someone interfered, so it refuses.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
question: An attacker briefly hijacks example.com's DNS records at the registrar. What can they most likely do?
options: Obtain a valid DV certificate for example.com via a DNS or HTTP challenge, since they now control the name
Nothing, because certificates require company paperwork
Only read existing traffic
Revoke example.com's current certificate
explain: DV issuance trusts whoever controls the domain at validation time. CAA does not help if the attacker can also change the CAA record. CT monitoring is how the real owner finds out (lesson 12).

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
question: A site sends HSTS with max-age of one year. A user who visited last week is now on a malicious Wi-Fi and types `site.example`. What happens?
options: The first request goes out over HTTP and can be stripped
The browser upgrades to HTTPS internally before sending anything, so there is no plain request to strip
The browser asks the user whether to use HTTPS
HSTS does not apply to typed URLs
explain: The stored policy makes the browser rewrite the scheme itself. The remaining gap is a user who has never visited (or whose policy expired), which preloading closes.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Post-quantum key exchange: ML-KEM hybrids in TLS
question: Why does TLS use a hybrid (X25519 plus ML-KEM) instead of ML-KEM alone?
options: ML-KEM cannot produce a 32-byte secret
Because X25519 is quantum-safe
So the connection stays secure if either algorithm holds: against quantum attackers via ML-KEM, and against a future classical break of the young ML-KEM via X25519
To make the ClientHello smaller
explain: Hybrids hedge both risks. The combined secret feeds the key schedule, so an attacker must break both components to recover the keys.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Tiled matmul: 2D pointer blocks, tl.dot and grouped ordering
question: In the grouped-ordering code, what ordering do you get with GROUP_SIZE_M = 1?
options: Column-major: tiles go down each column of C first
Plain row-major: pid_m = pid // num_pid_n and pid_n = pid % num_pid_n
A random permutation of tiles
Every program computes tile (0, 0)
explain: With G = 1, num_pid_in_group = num_pid_n, so group_id = pid // num_pid_n becomes pid_m and pid_n = pid % num_pid_n. Each group is one full row of tiles: exactly row-major order.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
question: A colleague changes the mask so the text token 'cube' (before BOI) can attend to p1 to p4 during training. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, more attention is always better
Information leaks: training uses image content that will not exist when 'cube' is generated, so train and inference disagree
The model runs out of memory
The image patches can no longer see the text
explain: At inference the caption comes before the image, so when 'cube' is produced there are no patches yet. A mask that lets 'cube' read them teaches the model to rely on information it will never have. The fix is to keep the rows before BOI strictly causal.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
question: A team runs an unmodified Linux nginx binary on a unikernel through its binary compatibility layer and sees less gain than the papers report. What is the most likely reason?
options: Binary compatibility disables the hypervisor's virtio drivers
nginx needs fork, which unikernels emulate with slow VM cloning
The binary is compiled for user mode and cannot run in kernel mode
Each syscall instruction still has to be trapped and translated, which costs far more than a direct function call
explain: The unmodified binary still executes syscall instructions, which the unikernel must catch and dispatch: 84 cycles versus 4 for a direct call in Unikraft's measurement. Linking the application against musl and the syscall shim turns those into direct calls.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue
question: Why does a unikernel coded against uknetdev in polling mode handle millions of packets per second where an interrupt-per-packet design does not?
options: It checks the ring in a loop and moves packets in bursts, so it pays no interrupt or notification per packet
Polling makes each descriptor smaller
Polling lets the guest write directly to the physical network card
Polling disables the hypervisor's isolation
explain: The ring itself is just memory. Per-packet costs come from notifications: interrupts into the guest and kicks out of it. Polling and burst APIs remove them from the hot path, at the price of a core that spins.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
question: Which property does UKL keep that a MirageOS unikernel gives up?
options: A single address space for the application and kernel
Multi-core execution and other processes running beside the linked application
Running the application at supervisor privilege
Static linking of the application with the kernel
explain: UKL links one application into Linux at supervisor privilege, like a unikernel, but keeps Linux's SMP support and lets ordinary processes run beside it. Mirage runs one vCPU and one program per VM.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
question: Your 768-d fp32 index needs 31 GB and the machine has 16 GB for page cache. Which change most directly attacks the latency cliff?
options: Switch the vectors to the cached tier so they are pre-loaded at startup
Use a faster SIMD instruction set
Increase the number of segments
Compress the vectors (for example to int8 or PQ codes) so the navigation data fits in RAM, and re-rank with full vectors
explain: Pre-loading cannot fit 31 GB into 16 GB, and SIMD speed is irrelevant when waiting on the SSD. Shrinking what the search touches per hop, and reading exact vectors only for the final re-rank, is exactly the DiskANN-style pattern.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
question: In the naive grouping on 8 GPUs (train 1-4-2, gen 1-2-2-2), why must G2 keep extra memory after the transition?
options: G2 is a pipeline boundary and must buffer activations
Its generation half (q3+q4) does not contain its training quarter (q2), so q2 must be kept for the next training stage
G2 hosts the controller
Consecutive grouping doubles the KV cache on even ranks
explain: Under consecutive TP grouping, G2 is rank 1 of [G1,G2] and gets q3+q4. Its training shard q2 is not inside that, so it must be stored separately until training resumes. The paper marks G2, G3, G6 and G7 as the GPUs with this redundancy.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Shrinking each frame: spatial pooling, SlowFast and time positions
question: Video-ChatGPT keeps T + N tokens by averaging over space and over time separately. Which question is it worst at?
options: What objects appear in the video?
Is the video indoors or outdoors?
Did the person pick up the cup before or after opening the door?
What is the overall topic of the video?
explain: The N spatial tokens are averaged over all frames, and the T temporal tokens are each one averaged vector per frame. Fine spatial detail tied to a specific moment is blurred, which hurts ordering questions about small actions.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Keep S = 256 tokens per frame and double the clip from 16 to 32 frames. What happens to the attention pair counts?
options: Every term doubles, so the ratio stays at 15.1
Spatial pairs double to 2,097,152, temporal pairs quadruple to 262,144, full attention quadruples to 67,108,864
Spatial pairs quadruple and temporal pairs double
Nothing changes because attention is per frame
explain: Spatial is T S squared, linear in T. Temporal is S T squared, quadratic in T but small while T is much less than S. Full is (TS) squared. The ST total is 2,359,296, so the advantage grows to TS/(S+T) = 28.4x.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
question: A team wants to train an RL agent for an Atari game cheaply using imagined experience, and they can collect actions and rewards by playing. Which approach fits best?
options: A model-based RL world model trained on their own action-labelled transitions, such as DreamerV3 or DIAMOND
A Genie-style model trained on unlabelled internet video, since labels are unnecessary
A text-to-video model prompted with the game's name
No world model: imagined experience cannot train agents
explain: When actions and rewards are available, action-conditioned world models built for RL (DreamerV3's latent imagination, DIAMOND's diffusion model with an Atari 100k mean HNS of 1.46) are the direct fit. Genie's latent actions solve a different problem: learning control from video with no labels.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: A hospital fine-tunes an ImageNet-21k ViT on 3,000 X-rays from scanner A; it will be deployed on scanner B, which produces visibly different images. Which plan best matches the evidence in this lesson?
options: Full fine-tune with a randomly initialized head, since it has the highest in-distribution accuracy
Train only the position embeddings
LP-FT: fit the head on frozen features first, then fine-tune all layers
Skip training and use the ImageNet head directly
explain: Deployment shift is exactly where Kumar et al. found fine-tuning from a random head loses to probing, and where LP-FT won on 10 of 10 OOD datasets. The ImageNet head predicts ImageNet classes, and position embeddings alone cannot learn new classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
question: A bimanual robot (14 action dims) runs at 50 Hz. How many tokens does per-step 256-bin tokenization need for a 1-second chunk?
explain: 14 dims x 50 steps = 700 tokens, matching the FAST paper's shirt-folding row. FAST needed about 53 for the same chunk.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: In the VQ-VAE loss, which parameters receive gradient from the middle term $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$?
options: The encoder only
The decoder only
Both the encoder and the codebook
The codebook only
explain: sg blocks the gradient to z_e, so only the codebook vectors e are updated by this term. The paper states: the decoder optimises the first term, the encoder the first and last, and the embeddings the middle term.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: You can either double the codebook from 8192 to 16,384 codes or halve the number of image tokens from 1024 to 512. Which choice reduces the stage 2 transformer's attention compute more, and why?
options: Doubling the codebook, because a larger softmax is the dominant cost
They are equivalent, since both change bits per image by the same factor
Halving tokens, because attention pairs scale with the square of sequence length while codebook size adds only one bit per token
Neither changes compute
explain: Halving T cuts attention pairs by 4x and bits per image by 2x. Doubling K adds 1 bit per token (13 to 14) and enlarges the embedding and output layers, but leaves sequence length, and thus attention cost, unchanged.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
question: A model mixes a backend that reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Does the runner reorder?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes, with threshold 1. The runner takes the minimum and ignores None
Only on steps that contain no prefills
explain: `calculate_reorder_batch_threshold` reduces with a min that skips None. One batch order is shared by all layers, so the smallest threshold wins, and backends that need no order are unaffected.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: Qwen2-VL's model card says the default visual-token range is 4 to 16,384 per image and suggests setting max_pixels to 1280 x 28 x 28 to save memory. What happens to a 12-megapixel phone photo under that setting?
options: It is resized, keeping its aspect ratio, so that it fits the pixel budget, and costs about 1,230 tokens instead of about 15,500
It is rejected because it exceeds max_pixels
It is cut into 336 x 336 tiles and every tile is kept
Nothing changes because Qwen2-VL uses native resolution
explain: The resize rule scales the image down, preserving aspect ratio, until it fits within max_pixels, then rounds each side to a multiple of 28. A 3024 x 4032 photo becomes 840 x 1148: 1,230 merged tokens plus 2 markers. Native resolution only holds inside the configured pixel range.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
question: Why does a failed compare&swap make the consensus protocol work for any number of processes, while a lost test&set does not?
options: CAS is faster than test&set on modern hardware
CAS uses more memory, so it can store all inputs
test&set is not atomic
A failed CAS returns the stored value, which is the winner's input; a lost test&set returns only a bit
explain: The losers' problem is identifying the winner. CAS writes the winner's value into the shared word and hands it back to every loser. test&set returns 1 to every loser and carries no identity.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
question: A 0.25 degree latitude-longitude grid covers 90N to 90S. Why does it have 721 rows instead of 720?
options: Because ERA5 adds one row of padding for convolutions
Because both poles are grid rows, so there are 720 intervals and 721 edges
Because the equator is stored twice, once per hemisphere
Because 721 is required to make the grid divisible by 4
explain: 180 degrees divided by 0.25 gives 720 intervals; counting the endpoints 90N and 90S gives 721 rows. Longitude wraps around, so 0 and 360 are the same column and there are exactly 1440.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Uncertainty: GenCast's diffusion ensembles and CRPS
question: Why does GenCast start each forecast step from fresh noise rather than from the previous step's output plus a small perturbation?
options: Diffusion models cannot accept conditioning inputs
Sampling from noise each step lets the model draw a new plausible state from the learned conditional distribution, giving sharp, distinct members
Noise makes the model run faster on TPUs
It removes the need for ERA5 initial conditions
explain: The diffusion model represents p(X(t+1) given X(t), X(t-1)). Each fresh noise draw yields a different sample of that distribution, so trajectories diverge realistically. The previous states still enter as conditioning, and forecasts still start from ERA5 plus perturbations.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: The intercepting proxy: Burp Suite and ZAP as a workflow
question: Which proxy feature is safe to leave running against a bounty target while you browse normally?
options: Passive scanning of the traffic you already send
Active scan
Intruder with a large wordlist
An automated crawler at maximum speed
explain: Passive scanning only reads the requests and responses you already generate; ZAP describes it as not changing the messages and safe to use. Active scans, Intruder runs and fast crawls send new traffic that the policy may forbid.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
question: After entering a password, an app redirects to /mfa. You request /account directly instead and get your account page. Which WSTG test does this fall under?
options: WSTG-ATHN-04 bypassing the authentication schema
WSTG-ATHN-03 lockout
WSTG-SESS-02 cookie attributes
WSTG-IDNT-04 account enumeration
explain: Skipping a step by calling a later page directly is the forced-browsing case WSTG-ATHN-04 describes. The fix is a server-side check of authentication state on every protected page.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Blind SSRF, out-of-band checks and server-side browsers
question: Burp Collaborator records an HTTP request from the target's servers after you submit a webhook URL. What have you shown so far?
options: That the server fetches attacker-supplied URLs, which may be intended; impact depends on what else it can reach
A critical SSRF
Remote code execution
Nothing, since external requests are normal
explain: PortSwigger notes an external interaction doesn't always indicate a vulnerability. For a webhook it is the feature. The finding needs impact: reaching internal services, reading responses, or bypassing a restriction.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
question: A programme scores your finding lower than you expected. What is the most effective response?
options: Explain, on the report, the specific impact or CVSS metric you think was misjudged, with evidence, and accept the final decision
Publish the bug to pressure them
Open a support ticket with the company
Submit the same bug again as a new report
explain: Programmes like GitLab let reporters raise concerns about a metric on the report itself, while the final decision rests with them. Going around the report, publishing or resubmitting breaks the rules.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
question: Which statement about the same-origin policy is true?
options: It applies only to https pages
It stops script injected into your own pages from reading your cookies
It keeps localStorage separate per origin
It prevents other sites from sending POST requests to your server
explain: Storage such as localStorage and IndexedDB is partitioned by origin. SOP does not stop cross-origin writes such as form POSTs, does nothing against script running inside your origin (XSS), and applies to http and https alike.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS with credentials, and the misconfigurations that leak data
question: An API trusts any origin that fully matches the regular expression `https://.*example\.com`. Which origin would it wrongly trust?
options: https://app.example.com
http://app.example.com
https://hackersexample.com
https://example.com
explain: The .* before example.com matches any characters, including none and including no dot, so hackersexample.com matches. The http origin fails because the pattern requires https. Exact comparison against a list avoids both mistakes.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: HTTPS, mixed content and HSTS: keeping the network out
question: A site sends `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000` in a response served over plain HTTP. What does the browser do?
options: Upgrades this one response to HTTPS
Stores it but only for the current session
Ignores the header, because HSTS is only accepted over HTTPS
Stores the host as HSTS for a year
explain: Browsers ignore HSTS sent over HTTP. Otherwise a MitM could inject a header for a site that does not support HTTPS (locking users out) or strip and replace it. The header must arrive over a secure connection to count.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The map: which bug class gets around which rule
question: Which pairing of bug class and the rule it gets around is correct?
options: Clickjacking gets around CSP script-src
postMessage bugs are fixed by HSTS
Firesheep got around Site Isolation
CORS misconfiguration is a server telling the browser to relax the same-origin policy for the wrong origin
explain: A CORS misconfiguration is the site itself switching off SOP's read protection for origins it should not trust. Clickjacking abuses embedding (fixed by framing headers), Firesheep abused unencrypted transport (fixed by HTTPS, Secure and HSTS), and postMessage bugs need code fixes.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
question: Which of these is a privilege (in the token) rather than a permission (in an object's DACL)?
options: Read access on the Reports folder for the Sales group
Deny Write on a registry key for Guests
Full control on a service for Administrators
Debug programs (SeDebugPrivilege)
explain: Privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege are listed in the access token and apply across the system. The others are ACEs on particular objects.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: LSASS: why attackers dump its memory, and how Windows protects it
question: A server was fully patched against EternalBlue, yet NotPetya still infected it. According to CISA, what is the most likely route?
options: A zero-day in NTFS
Clearing the Security log
A UAC prompt the admin accepted
Credentials stolen from LSASS on another machine, then used with PsExec or WMIC
explain: CISA describes credential theft with a modified Mimikatz plus PsExec or WMIC as NotPetya's first and most effective method. Patches do not stop valid credentials.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Sysmon and Microsoft Defender: deeper telemetry, built-in defence
question: You want to know which program opened lsass.exe at 02:10 last night. Which source is designed for that?
options: Security event 4720
Defender event 5007
System event 7045
Sysmon event 10 (ProcessAccess)
explain: Sysmon's ProcessAccess event records one process opening another, and Microsoft's documentation names reading LSASS memory as the use case. It needs a config that includes it, with filters for noise.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: First look at domains and Active Directory
question: Why do attackers who land on one workstation in a domain usually aim for Domain Admins rather than staying local?
options: Local admin rights do not exist in a domain
Domain Admins accounts have no SID
Kerberos is turned off for local accounts only
Domain Admins members can control every machine in the domain, so one account gives the whole network
explain: Domain Admins (RID 512) can administer every domain-joined machine and the DCs. Getting there turns one foothold into control of the organisation.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
question: An attacker has recorded one WPA2-Personal handshake. Which defence actually slows their offline guessing?
options: Turning on the AP's lockout after 5 failed logins
Hiding the SSID
Having chosen a passphrase with many more bits of randomness
Rebooting the AP
explain: Offline guessing never touches the AP, so lockouts and reboots do nothing, and the SSID is already in the recording. Only the size of the space the passphrase was drawn from, and the per-guess cost, set the attacker's time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: KRACK and FragAttacks: when the standard itself is wrong
question: Why does reinstalling an in-use key break CCMP's security, even though the key itself stays secret?
options: It disables the MIC
The reinstall reveals the key on the air
It resets the packet counter used as the nonce, so frames are encrypted under the same key and nonce again, repeating keystream
It downgrades CCMP to WEP
explain: CCMP (like any counter-mode scheme) is safe only while key and nonce pairs never repeat. Resetting the counter to 1 under the same key repeats them. It is the same keystream reuse that broke WEP in lesson 2.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor
question: Why did Apple add exponential restart throttling to BlastDoor and imagent?
options: Because Swift crashes more often
To save battery
Because many zero-click exploits need to crash a service many times (for example to break ASLR); doubling the restart delay stretches minutes into hours
To stop spam
explain: Project Zero's analysis: crash-oracle techniques learn memory layout by repeatedly crashing a service. With delays doubling up to about 20 minutes, such an exploit would need hours to roughly half a day.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
question: Why does Android's pinning documentation insist on a backup pin?
options: To allow user CAs
To double the encryption strength
Because if the pinned key must change (key rotation or a CA change), an app with only one pin cannot connect until users install an update
Because Android requires exactly two pins
explain: A pin is a hard rule in shipped code. If the server key changes and no other pinned key matches, every installed copy fails closed. A pre-generated backup key, pinned in advance, keeps you able to rotate.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
question: A pool runs 8 workers on 2 microseconds tasks, and its single locked queue costs 0.5 microseconds of serialized work per task. Using the lesson's model, about how many workers can the queue keep busy?
options: All 8, since 2 us tasks are much longer than 0.5 us
About 5, since (s + c)/c = 2.5/0.5 = 5
About 2, since only one thread can hold the lock
About 4, since half the time is spent in the queue
explain: The queue hands out at most 1/c = 2 tasks per microsecond, and each worker consumes 1/(s+c) = 0.4 tasks per microsecond, so the queue saturates at 2/0.4 = 5 workers. The other 3 mostly wait on the lock.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: A Tokio runtime has 8 workers and 4 of them are currently searching. A fifth idle worker tries to start searching. What happens?
options: It starts searching; there is no limit
It wakes all other parked workers first
It is refused, because 2 x 4 >= 8, so it goes back to parking
It steals from the global queue only
explain: transition_worker_to_searching returns false when 2 x num_searching >= num_workers, so at most about half the workers search at once. Tokio calls the limit sloppy on purpose: it is a throttle, not an exact bound.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data
question: Why can 1-sqrt beat linear for the same cooldown length?
options: It reaches low LR earlier in the cooldown, giving more steps for the bouncing to settle, at the cost of a little river progress
It keeps the LR near peak for longer during the cooldown
It never reaches zero, so the model keeps learning
It is identical to cosine to 10%
explain: Halfway through the cooldown 1-sqrt is at 0.293 of peak versus 0.5 for linear. Its average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 versus 1/2, so it gives up some area (river progress) in exchange for more time at small LR to shrink the hill part.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
question: A server reads each file with read() into a 64 KiB buffer, then write()s it to a TCP socket. Hot files are always in the page cache. Which costs does the read/write loop add that an in-kernel transfer would avoid?
options: The DMA from disk into the page cache
Two CPU copies per byte and two system calls per chunk
The DMA from the socket buffer to the NIC
Nothing: the page cache already makes it zero-copy
explain: With hot files there is no disk DMA at all, and the NIC DMA is needed by every method. What the loop adds is the copy page cache to user buffer, the copy user buffer to socket buffer, and a read plus a write per chunk. The page cache avoids disk reads, not memory copies.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
question: Kafka serves fetches with sendfile. A cluster enables TLS between clients and brokers. What happens to the zero-copy path?
options: Kafka stops using sendfile, since TLS runs in user space and the bytes must be encrypted there
Nothing, sendfile encrypts automatically
sendfile switches to splice
The broker uses MSG_ZEROCOPY instead
explain: Kafka's design docs say sendfile is not used when SSL is enabled, because the TLS library lives in user space. Kernel TLS can restore an in-kernel path, but encryption still reads every byte unless a NIC offloads it.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
question: An auto-tagger publishes tags without human review, and a wrong tag is costly while a missing tag is cheap. How should you set the threshold?
options: Use 0.5, since the scores are probabilities
Pick the threshold that maximizes recall
Use multi_label=False and always take the top label
On a labeled dev set, pick the lowest threshold that reaches the precision target, then confirm on a held-out test split
explain: When false positives are expensive, you constrain precision and take as much recall as that allows. 0.5 has no special meaning for these scores (T3 complaint scored 0.574 and was wrong). Always taking the top label guarantees a tag even when none applies.
